summary: This article (dated September 5, 2023) surveys African creation folklore, showing how diverse ethnic groups explain the origins of the world, people, and animals through gods, spirits, and ancestral heroes. It covers Yoruba, Kuba, Kongo, Dogon, and Zulu myths, the symbolic role of animals, the sacred role of griots and storytellers, and recurring themes of duality and balance. It ends by noting a modern resurgence of these myths in film, books, animation, and video games.
one_line: A 2023 overview of African creation myths from the Yoruba, Kuba, Kongo, Dogon, and Zulu, their storytellers, themes, and modern revival.
key_facts: The article is dated September 5, 2023 and treats African creation stories as a tapestry woven from countless societies and eras.
Anthropologist James Okoye says African creation myths are 'as varied as the landscape of the continent itself.'
In Yoruba mythology, the supreme god Olodumare sent the deity Orunmila to create the Earth, and life was then fashioned from the vast waters by Oduduwa, Orunmila's brother.
The Kuba Kingdom of Central Africa tells that the world began under the sea, where the supreme god Mbombo vomited the sun, moon, stars, and then the animals and people.
In the Boshongo creation myth of the Kongo people, the god Bumba, suffering from stomach pain, spews out the sun, moon, and stars and then creates the first men and animals from his vomit.
Folklorist Nia Mbwana of the University of Nairobi says animals in African myths symbolize traits from wisdom and cunning to strength and benevolence.
Oral tradition is preserved by griots, elders, and shamans through song, dance, and narrative.
Malian griot Sira Ba says, 'To tell a story is to water the roots of the tree of life.'
The Dogon tribe of Mali tells of Amma, the supreme god, who fashioned the world into a cosmic egg containing twin pairs of nommo spirits representing duality.
The Dogon's knowledge of Sirius B, a star invisible to the naked eye, is cited as evidence of astronomical lore in their creation myth.
The Zulu god Unkulunkulu is believed to have emerged from the reeds and created everything from ants to elephants, as well as the first humans.
Nigerian scholar Dr. Chukwudi Eze says the myths serve as 'an ethical compass' for living harmoniously with the community and environment.
Animation studios in Lagos, movie producers in Nairobi, and novelists in Johannesburg are reimagining these myths through books, films, and video games.
